summary: This RFC specifies the Internet Reliable Transaction Protocol, offered to the DARPA research community for reactions. It is an experimental transaction-oriented protocol that asks for discussion and suggestions.

plainLanguage.summary: A way for one computer to ask a quick question of another and get a reliable answer back, without the longer setup a phone call needs.

transaction protocol for the arpa internet
how does irtp compare to tcp
how does irtp handle reliable delivery
subtitle: A simple reliable delivery protocol between two hosts for transaction-based applications.

tldr.problem: Applications need a reliable, sequenced way to send packets between two hosts, but do not need the complexity of a full connection-oriented protocol like TCP. They also need to send multiple transactions and may communicate with many other hosts.
tldr.mechanism: IRTP provides packet-by-packet reliable delivery with sequence numbers and acknowledgments, synchronization via SYNCH messages, retransmission of lost packets, and multiplexing of data streams from different application ports on the same host pair connection.
tldr.outcome: Applications can send transaction-oriented messages reliably without TCP's overhead. The protocol is simpler to implement but requires less state management than connection-oriented protocols.

today: RFC 938 is an Experimental protocol from February 1985 that proposes a transaction-oriented reliable transport layer. It has not been widely deployed and remains experimental; TCP and UDP are the predominant transport protocols on the modern Internet.

sections.title: A Simpler Reliable Protocol
sections.content:
The Internet Reliable Transaction Protocol (IRTP) is designed for applications that need reliable, sequenced delivery of data between two hosts, but do not need the complexity of TCP. Unlike TCP, which is connection-oriented and handles individual data streams between specific processes (ports), IRTP maintains one host-to-host connection and delivers packets (transactions) reliably.

IRTP is simpler than TCP in that it sequences data on a packet-by-packet basis rather than as a character stream, and maintains only one connection between any two Internet addresses. This simplicity comes at the cost of less flexibility for concurrent multi-port communication, but allows one host to reliably communicate with many other hosts using minimal state information.
sections.plainLanguage: IRTP promises to deliver your message and deliver it in the right order, like a reliable mail service. But it does not set up a long phone call like TCP does; each message is just one package.

sections.title: Packet Structure
sections.content:
Every IRTP packet has an 8-byte header followed by optional data octets. The header contains five fields:

  • Packet Type: One of five types: SYNCH (0), SYNCH ACK (1), DATA (2), DATA ACK (3), or PORT NAK (4).
  • Port Number: For multiplexing data from different application protocols on the same host-to-host connection.
  • Sequence Number: A 16-bit unsigned integer identifying this packet, incremented for each new packet sent.
  • Length: Total octets in the packet including header and data (minimum 8).
  • Checksum: One's complement checksum over header and data.

The packet type determines the meaning of the sequence number and the port field.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message has a label saying what kind of message it is, who it is for, a number so you know which one it is, how big it is, and a check to make sure it did not get scrambled.

sections.title: Connection Synchronization and Data Transfer
sections.content:
The first time two hosts communicate, they exchange SYNCH packets to establish initial sequence numbers. The initiating host sends a SYNCH packet and waits for a SYNCH ACK reply. Once the handshake completes, both hosts are in data_transfer state and can send and receive DATA packets.

Each side maintains a send sequence number (incremented with each packet sent) and an expected next receive sequence number (rcv_nxt). As DATA packets arrive, the receiver sends back DATA ACK or PORT NAK acknowledgments with the value of rcv_nxt, confirming receipt of all packets up to that number. At most 8 unacknowledged packets (MAXPACK) may be outstanding in one direction at any time. If synchronization is lost due to a reboot, the host can re-establish it by sending another SYNCH.
sections.plainLanguage: First, both computers agree on starting numbers. Then they send packages, and each one says back "I got up to number X." If too many packages are waiting for an answer, you have to wait before sending more.

sections.title: Ports and Multiplexing
sections.content:
IRTP port numbers identify higher-level protocols (such as different application protocols) that share a single host-to-host connection. A process claims a port number to identify which application protocol it implements. Multiple processes can run on one host, each claiming different port numbers, and all communicate through a single IRTP connection to a remote host.

When a host receives a DATA packet on a port it does not recognize, it sends a PORT NAK acknowledgment to inform the sender that the port is not available. This differs from TCP, where a connection is made to a specific port; here, the entire connection between two hosts is one, and ports multiplex different applications within that connection.
sections.plainLanguage: Port numbers are like mailboxes at an apartment building. One connection between two buildings carries mail for many mailboxes. If you send to a mailbox that is not there, you get a message back saying so.

sections.title: Retransmission and Loss Detection
sections.content:
IRTP ensures reliable delivery through periodic retransmission of unacknowledged packets. The sender maintains a retransmission queue and periodically resends the oldest unacknowledged packet (the one with sequence number snd_una) until an acknowledgment confirms its receipt.

The RFC identifies a challenging aspect: IRTP modules continuously "ping" (retry) connections that are in use, even if the remote host appears unreachable. The document suggests mechanisms to distinguish between recoverable timeouts (retrying quickly) and apparent host unreachability (retrying slowly at PINGTIME intervals), allowing applications to be notified when a destination becomes unreachable and when it recovers.
sections.plainLanguage: If you do not get an answer, you send the message again. If you keep not getting an answer, you slow down and try less often, but you never stop trying completely.

fields.name: Packet Type
fields.desc: Message type: SYNCH, SYNCH ACK, DATA, DATA ACK, or PORT NAK.

fields.name: Sequence Number
fields.desc: Packet sequence number, incremented with each DATA packet sent.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Total length of packet in octets, including header.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: One's complement sum checksum over header and data.
